title: Instruction Types & Classes
summary: The families of instructions every ISA needs, and how a simple `if` statement compiles down to them.

slides.markdown:
**Data-movement instructions** shuffle values between memory and registers without computing anything new: **loads** (memory → register), **stores** (register → memory), and **register moves** (register → register).

In a load/store ISA these are the *only* instructions allowed to touch memory — every arithmetic or logic operation must first have its operands already sitting in registers. That's the load/store discipline showing up again here, as a concrete instruction-family rule rather than an abstract principle.

**Arithmetic and logic instructions** are the ALU's job list: `add`, `sub`, `mul`, `and`, `or`, `xor`, shifts. Each one also typically sets **condition flags** as a side effect — zero, carry, overflow, negative — even when the program never explicitly asks for them.

Those flags matter beyond the instruction that set them: the *very next* conditional branch usually reads them to decide whether to take a jump. This is exactly how a compiled `if` connects a comparison to a branch — through flags, not through some hidden channel.

**Control-flow instructions** redirect the program counter instead of computing a value: **branches** (conditional, based on flags), **jumps** (unconditional), **calls** (jump + save a return address), and **returns** (jump back to that saved address).

Every loop, `if`, and function call in a high-level language ultimately becomes one of these four. Calls and returns specifically are what make function boundaries real at the hardware level — the CPU has no concept of "functions," only jumps with a remembered address to come back to.

slides.subTitle: How if compiles down
slides.markdown:
An `if (x > y)` compiles into two cooperating instructions: a **comparison** (often just a subtraction whose result is discarded but whose flags are kept) followed by a **conditional branch** that reads those flags.

```
cmp  x, y        ; computes x - y, sets flags (no result kept)
bgt  label       ; branch to label if flags say "greater than"
```

This two-step pattern — set flags, then branch on them — is the mechanical reality behind every `if`, `while`, and `for` a programmer writes.

A concrete C-to-assembly trace:

```c
if (a > b) { x = 1; } else { x = 2; }
```

```asm
cmp  a, b
ble  else_label       ; branch if a <= b
mov  x, 1
jmp  end_label
else_label:
mov  x, 2
end_label:
```

Notice the compiler **inverted the condition** (`a > b` became a branch on `a <= b`) so the fall-through path handles the "true" branch and a jump skips the "false" branch — a routine compiler pattern for minimizing jumps.

Conditional branches aren't free — a mispredicted branch flushes a pipelined CPU's in-flight work. Many ISAs offer an alternative for short conditionals:

| | Conditional branch | Predicated / conditional-move |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | Jump or don't, based on flags | Execute both paths' data; select result at the end |
| Misprediction cost | High in deep pipelines | None — no branch to mispredict |
| Best for | Long or unpredictable branch bodies | Tiny, cheap-to-compute both-sides code |

A compiler picks conditional-move over a branch specifically when both sides are trivial (e.g., `x = a > b ? a : b`) — the cost of computing the unused side is smaller than a likely misprediction.

slides.subTitle: Crossing into the kernel
slides.markdown:
**System instructions** — `syscall`/`trap`/`int` — deliberately hand control to the operating system instead of executing user logic directly. They exist because certain operations (touching a device, mapping memory, killing a process) are too dangerous to let arbitrary user code do unchecked; the instruction instead transfers execution to a fixed, trusted kernel entry point, switching the CPU's privilege level as it does.

This is the mechanism behind every file read, every `malloc` that needs more memory from the OS, and every process spawn — application code never touches hardware directly, it asks the kernel to do it via exactly this instruction class. Some ISAs add finer-grained privilege levels (hypervisor, secure/trusted zones) built on the same idea: an instruction that raises privilege only through one audited entry point, never arbitrarily.

slides.subTitle: One instruction, many data lanes
slides.markdown:
**SIMD** (single instruction, multiple data) instructions apply one operation across several data elements packed into a wide register at once — e.g., adding four 32-bit floats in one `paddd`-style instruction instead of four separate scalar adds. Modern ISAs dedicate wide register files and instruction sets specifically to this (SSE/AVX on x86, NEON/SVE on ARM, the V extension on RISC-V).

This is what makes **auto-vectorization** in optimizing compilers meaningful: a simple scalar loop over an array can be rewritten by the compiler into far fewer SIMD instructions doing the same total work, often the single biggest speedup available for data-parallel numeric code — image processing, physics, ML kernels — without changing a line of source.

slides.subTitle: Why an ordinary load and store can't build a lock
slides.markdown:
A plain load followed by a plain store ("read the value, add one, write it back") isn't safe across threads — another core can slip in between the load and the store and both cores compute the same stale increment, losing an update. **Atomic instructions** close that gap in one indivisible hardware step: **compare-and-swap (CAS)** checks a memory location still holds an expected value and, only if so, writes a new one, all as one uninterruptible operation; **load-linked/store-conditional (LL/SC)** achieves the same effect with a paired instruction sequence that fails the store if anything touched the address in between.

Every lock-free data structure, mutex implementation, and atomic counter in a language's standard library ultimately compiles down to one of these two primitives — there is no other way to safely read-modify-write shared memory across cores without falling back to a full lock.
